source.title: SpeechStew: Simply Mix All Available Speech Recognition Data to Train One Large Neural Network
source.authors: William Chan; Daniel S. Park; Chris Lee; Yu Zhang; Quoc V. Le; Mohammad Norouzi

record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream speech-recognition WER for SpeechStew models of two sizes, bearing on V6, but does not measure the original loss-scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own 100M-versus-1B WER results, which bear on downstream performance by scale (V6). It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or assess compute-optimal allocations. Results from prior work in Table 1 are not rows.
record.test_reason: This is a speech-recognition paper. Its main claim is that mixing public ASR datasets into one large Conformer gives near-SoTA WER. Model scale is used as a tool motivated by prior scaling results, not studied. Only two sizes appear (100M, 1B), and they also differ in wav2vec LibriLight pre-training, optimizer and batch size, so size is confounded. There is no loss measurement, no power-law fit and no prediction from loss or scale. The models are ASR systems, not text-pretrained language models, so the rows do not measure V6's downstream predictability of LMs. Two confounded points cannot show V5's power-law form in speech.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The main conclusion is that simply mixing all public ASR data to train one large model gives SoTA or near-SoTA WER without a language model, plus strong transfer to CHiME-6. On size, the 1B model improves on Common Voice and LibriSpeech but slightly degrades elsewhere; the authors suggest in-domain LibriLight pre-training may bias it. They also report that the 1B model transfers better to CHiME-6. No scaling-law claims are made.
record.recipe_differences: Speech recognition WER comparison across 100M and 1B Conformer models, not language-model held-out loss scaling or power-law fitting. The 1B model also uses LibriLight wav2vec pre-training.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size comparison varies by task; the 1B model has additional LibriLight wav2vec pre-training.

fits_no_version.finding: 1B vs 100M SpeechStew ASR WER, with size confounded by wav2vec LibriLight pre-training and the training recipe. The 1B model is better on Common Voice and LibriSpeech (e.g. other split 4.0→3.3). It is slightly worse on AMI, SWBD, CallHome and TED-LIUM (e.g. CallHome 8.3→10.6), and equal on WSJ (1.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing ASR model size (with confounded pre-training) does not uniformly improve downstream WER across domains.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2, CHiME-6 transfer: the 1B model beats the 100M model zero-shot (dev 39.2 vs 54.9; eval 53.7 vs 57.2) and after fine-tuning (dev 31.9 vs 33.1; eval 38.9 vs 40.6). No row records this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger ASR pretrained models transfer better to low-resource noisy tasks.

record.problems: Only two model sizes are compared, with different pretraining setups; the comparison does not isolate size. No held-out cross-entropy results, scaling-law fits, uncertainty estimates, or compute-optimal allocation analysis are reported.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss or scaling in parameters, tokens or compute.
Power-law form in speech: only two confounded model sizes, no fit.
All: no language models, no prediction from scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 labels were dropped. The subjects are ASR models rather than LMs, and the size comparison is confounded with wav2vec pre-training, optimizer and batch size. This is not a test of downstream predictability. Kaplan et al. is cited only in related work.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether power-law loss scaling holds in speech or other modalities/training regimes.
No prediction from pretraining loss; only one comparison between 100M and 1B models, with different pretraining setups.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices.
